newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen heading higher ahead of FOMC.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen heading higher ahead of FOMC.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to move higher at the start of trading Tuesday as the market gears up for the outcome of today's meeting of the Fed's Federal Open Market Committee.
Analysts said they expected some followthrough at the start from Monday's 100-point rally in the Dow industrials.

"Almost everyone has built in a rate hike of 25-basis points," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments. "The surprise will be if the Federal Reserve does not hike interest rates."
"If we do not get a rate hike there may be some unraveling of positions from yesterday to sell from buy," Cardillo said.
Larry Wachtel, analyst at Prudential Securities, said that after yesterday's rally, the question is "What do we do for an encore after going up 100 points?
"We will have to watch the techs to see whether stocks like Intel Corp and International Business Machines Corp can retain some stability after bouncing off the bottom yesterday," Wachtel said.
March consumer confidence data are due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average was up 395.79 points, or 2.19 percent, at 18,439.61.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was up 44.3 at 4259.1

Among U.S. shares traded in London, Motorola Corp was up 3/8 at 57-3/4 after the Wall Street Journal reported that the company was on the verge of winning a "potentially significant" digital celullar telephone contract in Japan.
Boeing Co, which signed a $685 million contract on Tuesday to sell jets to China, was up 3/8 at 106-1/8.
Philip Morris Cos Inc was up 1/4 at 116-1/8.
General Motors Corp added 1/8 to 58 after the company signed a long-awaited $1.57 billion joint venture to produce medium-sized cars in China.
The dollar crawled higher against the yen in Tokyo and was higher against the yen and mark in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were mostly higher, with the long bond up 3/32 to yield 6.92 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that Monday's flight from technologies was more bad news for networking companies, which were among the first to be hit by worries of too-high valuations and slowing growth.
The New York Times Market Place writes that companies that that are making money marketing variable annuities are even hotter than the annuities themselves.
